posts.copy:
354,000. That is how many industrial robots China installed in 2025, 59% of every new robot put to work worldwide.

The number is not the news. Who sold them is.

The International Federation of Robotics published the figures in September 2026. China's installations grew 20% in 2025 and beat the previous annual record by almost 60,000 units.

Chinese manufacturers supplied 195,000 of them, a 55% share of their home market. In 2024 that share was 57%.

Read from a desk in London or New York, the first number says China is automating and the second says foreign suppliers are being pushed out. Neither is quite right. Local brands now outsell foreign ones at home, and foreign brands still put in roughly 45% of a record year.

What that means for a buyer is a credible local option for most jobs, which changes every conversation about price and lead time. You only feel that on the ground, standing next to the integrator who quotes both.

A report gives you the share. It does not give you the room where the share gets decided.

If you want to see this on the ground for yourself, work with us.

posts.copy:
You can still debate whether humanoid robots are useful. You cannot debate who is shipping them.

Counterpoint Research counted more than 22,000 humanoid robots shipped worldwide in the first half of 2026, up nearly 300% on a year earlier.

One Chinese company, AgiBot, shipped around 9,700 of them. That is a share of over 43%.

The top five makers took 86% of everything shipped.

Read from a boardroom in London or New York, 9,700 robots in six months sounds like a pilot programme. It is the wrong frame.

A pilot is a handful of units on a test cell. Thousands of units in six months means actuators, reducers, sensors and battery packs arriving at that rate, from suppliers who are already tooled for it.

That supplier base is the part worth seeing. The robot is only the visible end of it, and it is the end every Western headline photographs.

The question for a Western operator has moved. It is no longer whether this works. It is who will already be building at scale when it does.

posts.copy:
In 2016 KFC and Pizza Hut had a little over 7,000 restaurants in China between them. By September 2026 KFC alone had 14,307.

The fried chicken did not do that. The ownership did.

In October 2016 Yum! Brands spun its China business off into a separate company, Yum China, listed in New York, with Primavera Capital and Ant Financial putting in $460 million.

From then on Yum China was the franchisee, a separate company built around one market, setting its own pace.

→ Pace. 1,706 net new stores in 2025, then 692 in the third quarter of 2026, a quarterly record.
→ Channel. Delivery was around 48% of company sales in 2025, up from 39% a year earlier.
→ Partners. By September 2026, 19% of stores were run by franchisees.

Not every number rose. Same-store sales fell 3% in that quarter. The store count kept climbing anyway, to 19,989.

The unlock was structure. What Yum! Brands did not do was keep China as one line on a global plan.

Who owns the market is a go-to-market decision before it is a legal one, and it is usually the first thing we test in GTM advisory.

We have never worked with Yum! Brands or Yum China. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
In 2022 Coca-Cola's biggest cola in India was not called Coca-Cola. It got there in three stages, and the first one was a mistake.

1/ Buy the local leader. In 1993 Coca-Cola bought the soft drinks portfolio of Parle's Ramesh Chauhan, and Thums Up came with it.

2/ Starve it. By Chauhan's account, Coca-Cola gave Thums Up no budget at all for at least the first two years, and cut supplies where it was strong. Business Today reported Rs 200 crore going behind Coca-Cola itself.

3/ Back it. Later in the decade, support for Thums Up started scaling up. In February 2022 chief executive James Quincey told investors that Thums Up had become a $1 billion brand in India. Nielsen data cited by Business Today put Pepsi second, behind Thums Up.

The unlock was the local brand. What Coca-Cola eventually stopped doing was insisting the global one had to win.

That is the uncomfortable version of localisation. Sometimes the asset you need in a market already belongs to it, and the hard part is letting it lead.

The answer is different in each of APAC's 15+ ecosystems, which is why it is one of the first things we test in GTM advisory.

We have never worked with Coca-Cola. This is commentary from the outside.

posts.copy:
When Maggi came back to India in November 2015, it came back in 100 towns, not everywhere. Not by accident, but by design.

In June 2015 India's food regulator had banned Maggi noodles. In August the Bombay High Court lifted the ban, subject to fresh tests.

What Nestlé did next was sequencing.

→ Tests first. Maggi passed tests by three government-accredited laboratories before it went back on sale.
→ Narrow first. It returned in 100 towns through 300-odd distributors, and stayed out of eight states where it was still not allowed.
→ Online first. Snapdeal sold out the first batch of 60,000 welcome kits within five minutes.

By October 2016 Nestlé said its share of India's instant noodle market was back to 57%, against 75% before the crisis. In its 2023-24 annual report Nestlé India said it sold over six billion servings of Maggi in the year, making India the largest Nestlé market for Maggi worldwide.

The unlock was the order of operations. What Nestlé did not do was relaunch nationally into a market that had not finished deciding whether to trust it.

Every APAC market has its own version of that ordering problem, and the right order differs across 15+ ecosystems. Mapping it comes first in our GTM advisory work.

We were not involved in Nestlé's recovery. This is commentary.

posts.copy:
American buyers were supposed to be finished with Hyundai by 1998. In 1999 its US sales rose 82%.

The reputation problem was real. When Hyundai first came to the US, NPR later wrote, the name was synonymous with poor quality. It became a punch line on late-night talk shows.

By 1998 its US sales were heading for their lowest level ever, about 90,000.

In September 1998 Hyundai Motor America changed what the buyer was being asked to believe.

→ A 10-year, 100,000-mile powertrain warranty, plus five years and 60,000 miles bumper to bumper.
→ No deductibles on any of it.
→ A name for it: America's Best Warranty.

Sales in 1999 came to 164,190, against 90,217 the year before, and the company named the warranty as one factor bringing buyers into showrooms. In 2025 Hyundai sold 901,686 vehicles in the US, a record for the third year running.

The buyer did not believe the product. The warranty moved the cost of that doubt from the buyer to the brand.

That is the pattern in most Asia-to-West moves: the buyer, the pricing and the story, rarely the product. Rebuilding those is what our GTM advisory is for.

We were not involved in Hyundai's expansion. This is commentary.

80,000. That is roughly how many US stores carried Bibigo's Korean range by August 2026.

The dumplings were never the hard part. Getting them into American freezers was.

In November 2018 CJ CheilJedang agreed to buy 80% of Schwan's Company, a US frozen-food maker founded in 1952, for $1.84 billion. CJ named what it was buying: logistics, distribution and sales networks throughout the entire US.

It did not try to build American grocery distribution for a Korean brand one buyer at a time. It bought a company whose brands, Red Baron and Tony's pizza among them, were already in those aisles.

What followed, per the Korea Herald in August 2026:

→ Bibigo dumplings led the US dumpling market with a 41% share in 2024.
→ CJ's US food revenue rose from 3.32 trillion won in 2020 to 4.91 trillion won in 2025.
→ The US made up 83% of its overseas revenue.

The buyer for a frozen dumpling in America is not a fan of Korean food. It is a category buyer deciding what earns a freezer door, and a distributor deciding what is worth a truck.

That is usually where an Asian brand stalls in the West: the route to the buyer.

Finding that route, and sometimes the partner to buy or borrow, is what our GTM advisory is for.

No relationship with CJ CheilJedang. Commentary only.

posts.copy:
Nobody wants to hear this, but Kikkoman won American kitchens by telling people to put soy sauce on meat.

In 1957 it set up a marketing company in San Francisco to break into the US market properly. The soy sauce was already the soy sauce. What changed was the story around it.

→ The label. In 1957 export bottles started carrying the words "ALL-PURPOSE SEASONING".
→ The pitch. A catchphrase, "Delicious on Meat", backed by in-store demonstrations at supermarkets.
→ The product. Teriyaki Sauce, sold from 1961, was launched in the US as a barbecue sauce.

Then the supply chain followed the demand. In 1973 full-scale production began at a plant in Walworth, Wisconsin. Kikkoman says its soy sauce is now made in nine overseas plants and sold in over 100 countries.

It did not ask American shoppers to learn Japanese cooking first. It walked into the dish they already made, in the aisle they already shopped.

That is the hard part of most Asia-to-West moves. Rarely the product. Usually the buyer, the pricing and the story, and the story most of all.

Rewriting that story for a buyer who has never heard of you is a large part of our GTM advisory work.

We had nothing to do with this one. We just think it is the clearest example around.

posts.copy:
Too many corporate study trips to China come home with a photo album and no decision. Not by accident, but by design.

Give us an hour with a strategy team planning one and we can usually tell which kind of trip it will be.

We start with four things:

→ The question
→ The visits
→ Who travels
→ The flight home

Then we look at what is underneath them.

Is there one decision this trip is meant to inform, written down before anyone books a flight?

Were the visits picked to answer that question, or because they were the famous names that said yes?

Is the person who will own the decision on the trip, or reading a summary of it a month later?

Who writes up what the team saw, and by when, before the urgency wears off?

From the inside, a trip that changed nothing looks like a trip to the wrong places. Sometimes it was. More often it left without a question, and no visit can answer a question nobody asked.

That is the part of OJV Educate we care about most. The week is built backwards from the decision.

If you are planning an executive trip to China and need it to end in a decision, not a deck, work with us.

posts.copy:
You can hand a founder's outbound to an agency. You cannot hand over the reason buyers were replying to a founder.

Give us an hour with a founder who still closes every deal and we can usually tell whether that pipeline survives a second seller.

We start with four things:

→ Who replies
→ Why they reply
→ What the founder says on the call
→ What is written down

Then we look at what is underneath them.

Are buyers answering because the message is good, or because the sender is the founder?

Could anyone else on the team explain in two sentences why your last five customers bought?

When a deal stalls, does the founder rescue it with a call nobody else could make?

Is any of that in a playbook, or only in one person's head and inbox?

From the inside, founder-led sales looks like a sales process. Often it is a set of relationships nobody has written down, so the first sales hire looks like the wrong hire.

Across APAC's 15+ ecosystems it gets harder, because what earned the reply in one market rarely earns it in the next.

If you are a founder still closing every deal yourself and need pipeline that does not depend on you, work with us.
